concepts.title: Neuron Structure and Resting Membrane Potential

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Neuron Structure and Resting Membrane Potential' refers to.
questions.a: A neuron has a cell body with cytoplasm and nucleus, dendrites carrying impulses toward the cell, and a long axon ending in synaptic knobs; the resting nerve membrane maintains a resting potential through the sodium potassium pump, keeping the outside positive and the inside negative.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Neuron Structure and Resting Membrane Potential'.
questions.a: The polarised resting membrane is maintained by active transport of three sodium ions out for two potassium ions in, making the axonal membrane more permeable to potassium ions at rest.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Neuron Structure and Resting Membrane Potential' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 18.1 Neural System, 18.2 Human Neural System, 18.3.1 Generation and Conduction of Nerve Impulse (source: kebo118.txt sections 18.1-18.3.1)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Synapse and Synaptic Transmission' refers to.
questions.a: At a synapse the axon terminal of one neuron meets the dendrite of another across a synaptic cleft; in chemical synapses calcium entry releases neurotransmitters like acetylcholine from synaptic vesicles that bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, while electrical synapses pass current directly at gap junctions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Synapse and Synaptic Transmission'.
questions.a: Chemical synapses are far more common, and neurotransmitter binding generates a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron, allowing one-way conduction across the cleft.

concepts.title: Human Brain, Reflex Action and Reflex Arc

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Human Brain, Reflex Action and Reflex Arc' refers to.
questions.a: The human brain divides into forebrain with cerebrum and limbic structures, midbrain and hindbrain with pons, cerebellum and medulla controlling involuntary functions; a reflex action such as the knee jerk travels through a reflex arc of receptor, sensory neuron, CNS centre, motor neuron and effector muscle, with the spinal cord as its centre.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Human Brain, Reflex Action and Reflex Arc'.
questions.a: The medulla controls vital involuntary functions like breathing and heart rate, while the cerebellum keeps posture and balance, and reflex arcs protect the body before conscious processing.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Human Brain, Reflex Action and Reflex Arc' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 18.4 Central Neural System, 18.5 Reflex Action and Reflex Arc (source: kebo118.txt sections 18.4, 18.5)
